title: 03. Databases & Data Modeling: Microsoft SQL Server
summary: Microsoft SQL Server is a commercial-grade RDBMS from Microsoft, characterized by T-SQL (Transact-SQL procedural extensions), Always On Availability Groups for HA/DR with up to 9 replicas (sync or async), columnstore indexes…
objectives: What is T-SQL and how does it differ from ANSI SQL?
How do Always On Availability Groups work?
What is a columnstore index and when should you use it?
What is In-Memory OLTP (Hekaton) and when is it useful?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Microsoft SQL Server is a **commercial-grade RDBMS** from Microsoft, characterized by **T-SQL** (Transact-SQL procedural extensions), **Always On Availability Groups** for HA/DR with up to 9 replicas (sync or async), **columnstore indexes** for blistering OLAP scan performance, **In-Memory OLTP** (Hekaton) for lock-free memory-optimized tables, and — since SQL Server 2017 — first-class **Linux and container support**, making it the relational backbone of the **enterprise Microsoft stack** (Windows, Active Directory, .NET, Azure) and increasingly cross-platform.

SQL Server occupies a distinct niche in the database world: it's the default RDBMS for organizations already committed to the Microsoft ecosystem — Windows Server, Active Directory, .NET, Azure, Office/Excel, Power BI, SharePoint. The integration story is unmatched: Windows Authentication (Kerberos/NTLM) gives single sign-on to the database; SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) is the most polished DB GUI; Power BI, Excel, and Analysis Services connect natively; Azure SQL Database is a fully-managed SQL Server in the cloud. For an enterprise running .NET applications on Windows with Windows-authenticated users, choosing SQL Server is the path of least resistance — and the licensing cost (often $7k–$25k per core for Enterprise edition) is justified by reduced integration friction. The trade-off: SQL Server is deeply optimized for the Microsoft stack; using it with Linux, Java, or non-Microsoft tooling works but loses much of the integration advantage. The 2017 Linux release (and Docker container support) broadened its appeal — you can now run SQL Server on Linux containers in Kubernetes, the same as PostgreSQL or MySQL — but the Microsoft-stack synergy remains its strongest selling point.

**T-SQL (Transact-SQL)** is SQL Server's dialect of SQL, extending ANSI SQL with procedural constructs: control flow (`IF`, `WHILE`, `BEGIN...END`), error handling (`TRY...CATCH`), variables (`DECLARE @x INT`), stored procedures, user-defined functions, and triggers. This makes SQL Server a "programmable database" — complex business logic can live in stored procedures, executed entirely server-side, with no network round-trips between the app and the DB. Trade-off: business logic in stored procedures is hard to version control (no git for SPs natively), hard to test (no unit test framework for T-SQL), and hard to refactor (no IDE refactor support). Modern practice is to keep business logic in the application (C#, Java, Python) and use T-SQL only for data manipulation — but many legacy SQL Server deployments have thousands of lines of T-SQL business logic that would be expensive to rewrite. T-SQL also has unique features: `OUTPUT` clause (returns affected rows like a RETURNING), `MERGE` (UPSERT in one statement), `PIVOT`/`UNPIVOT` (cross-tab aggregation), and window functions (which SQL Server had years before PostgreSQL).

**Always On Availability Groups** (introduced in SQL Server 2012) is the modern HA/DR solution, replacing the older Database Mirroring. An AG is a group of up to 9 replicas of one or more databases: one **primary** replica accepts writes; up to 8 **secondary** replicas are read-only. Replicas can be configured as **synchronous-commit** (zero data loss, requires low-latency network — typically same region) or **asynchronous-commit** (small data loss window, supports cross-region). Key features: (1) **Read-only routing** — the AG listener (a virtual network name) routes read-only connections to a secondary replica, offloading reads from the primary. (2) **Automatic failover** — with synchronous-commit secondaries, the AG automatically fails over in 5-30 seconds when the primary fails (requires a Windows Server Failover Cluster quorum, or none on Linux via Pacemaker). (3) **Multi-database AG** — a single AG can contain multiple databases that fail over together (important when databases are related via cross-database queries). (4) **Distributed AG** — chains AGs across regions for global DR. This is more flexible than PostgreSQL/MySQL replication (one primary + N read replicas) because AGs combine sync + async replicas, read routing, and multi-database atomic failover. Trade-off: AGs are complex to set up (Windows Server Failover Cluster, AD integration, Kerberos SPNs); on Linux, Pacemaker replaces WSFC.

**Columnstore indexes** are SQL Server's killer feature for analytical workloads. Traditional rowstore indexes (B-Tree) store data row-by-row — great for OLTP point lookups, terrible for OLAP scans (sum a column across 1B rows = read 1B rows). Columnstore indexes store data column-by-column: all values of column A are contiguous, all of column B, etc. Benefits: (1) **Massive compression** — similar values in a column compress well (run-length encoding, dictionary encoding). 1 TB rowstore typically compresses to 100-300 GB columnstore. (2) **Scan speed** — to sum column A, only column A's data is read; columns B, C, D aren't touched. A 100-column table scan reads 1/100th the I/O. (3) **Vectorized execution** — batch mode processes 1000 rows at a time in SIMD instructions, 10-100x faster than row mode. SQL Server supports both **clustered columnstore** (the entire table is columnstore — for pure OLAP) and **nonclustered columnstore** (columnstore index on a rowstore table — for hybrid HTAP). Trade-off: columnstore indexes are slower for single-row updates (batch delete + insert) — best for append-mostly workloads. Real-world: SQL Server columnstore powers many financial analytics, retail dashboards, and IoT aggregations where terabyte-scale scans must return in seconds.

**In-Memory OLTP (Hekaton)**, introduced in SQL Server 2014, provides memory-optimized tables and natively-compiled stored procedures for extreme-throughput OLTP. Memory-optimized tables live entirely in RAM (with a checkpoint file on disk for durability); they use a **lock-free, multi-version concurrency control** based on timestamps — no locks, no latches, no spinlocks. Native-compiled stored procedures are compiled to C and then to machine code, bypassing the SQL interpreter. Performance: 10-100x for the right workload (insert-heavy, simple lookups, no cross-table joins). Trade-offs: (1) Tables must fit in RAM (limited by hardware). (2) Limited T-SQL surface in native procs (no cursors, limited functions). (3) Schema changes are painful (must drop and recreate). (4) Doesn't help workloads that are bottlenecked on I/O or complex joins. In-Memory OLTP is a niche feature — useful for specific high-throughput scenarios (trading systems, real-time bidding, gaming state) but not generally applicable. Real-world: Microsoft's own internal billing uses In-Memory OLTP for the transaction-processing core; some trading firms use it for tick-data ingestion.

**SQL Server on Linux** (2017+) was a watershed moment. Microsoft ported SQL Server to Linux by wrapping the SQL Server engine in a translation layer (the "SQL Platform Abstraction Layer" or SQLPAL, derived from Drawbridge research) that maps Windows kernel calls to Linux equivalents. The same engine runs on Windows and Linux — same T-SQL, same features, same performance characteristics (within ~5%). Supported on Red Hat, SUSE, Ubuntu, and Docker. HA on Linux uses Pacemaker (replacing Windows Server Failover Cluster). This opened SQL Server to containerized deployments — SQL Server containers run on Kubernetes, integrate with cloud-native tooling, and break the previous "Windows only" assumption. Trade-off: some Windows-only features (Active Directory integration, certain SQL Agent features) require extra setup on Linux; the experience is best on Azure (where Microsoft manages the glue). Real-world: many shops now run SQL Server in Linux containers in AKS/EKS, treating it like any other stateful workload.

Real-world: large enterprises in finance, healthcare, retail, and government run SQL Server for their core OLTP systems. Examples: banks running trading systems on SQL Server with In-Memory OLTP (millions of transactions/sec); retailers using columnstore indexes for sales analytics over billions of rows; hospitals storing patient records with Always On AGs across data centers for HA. The enterprise Microsoft stack (Windows + AD + .NET + SQL Server + Power BI) is a cohesive, supported bundle that's hard to beat for organizations standardized on Microsoft. The trade-off: cost (Enterprise edition is expensive per-core), vendor lock-in (T-SQL dialect, Microsoft-specific features), and slower community innovation than PostgreSQL (pgvector took years to be matched in SQL Server's nascent vector support). For greenfield projects in non-Microsoft stacks, PostgreSQL or MySQL are usually better choices; for Microsoft-shop enterprises, SQL Server remains the default.

(OLTP)"] SQL -->|"columnstore"| Columnstore["Columnstore indexes
(OLAP scans)"] SQL -->|"memory-optimized"| Hekaton["In-Memory OLTP
(Hekaton, lock-free)"] SQL -->|"Always On AG"| AG["Availability Group"] AG --> Primary["Primary replica
(read-write)"] AG -->|"sync-commit"| Sec1["Secondary 1
(read-only, sync)"] AG -->|"async-commit"| Sec2["Secondary 2
(read-only, async, DR)"] AG --> Listener["AG Listener
(virtual network name)"] Listener -->|"read-write conn"| Primary Listener -->|"read-only conn"| Sec1 SQL -->|"Windows auth"| AD["Active Directory
(Kerberos SSO)"] SQL -->|"Linux/Pacemaker"| PM["Pacemaker
(HA cluster)"] ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` Always On Availability Group (3 replicas, mixed sync+async): +-------------------+ | AG Listener | (virtual name: sql-prod.contoso.com) | read-write -> P | clients connect to listener, not individual nodes | read-only -> S1 | +---------+---------+ | +--------+--------+--------+ | | | | v v v v +----+ +----+ +----+ | P | | S1 | | S2 | |(RW)| |(RO)| |(RO)| |sync|--->|sync| |async| | | | | | | | DC1| | DC1| | DC2| (S2 cross-region for DR) +----+ +----+ +----+ | ^ ^ +-------+--------+ Primary fails -> auto-failover to S1 (sync, zero data loss) 5-30 seconds, listener reroutes automatically Columnstore index (vs rowstore B-Tree): Rowstore (B-Tree, OLTP): Row1: [id=1, name="alice", city="NYC", age=30, ...] Row2: [id=2, name="bob", city="LA", age=25, ...] -> sum(age) reads ALL columns, lots of wasted I/O Columnstore (OLAP): id: [1, 2, 3, ...] (RLE compressed) name: ["alice","bob","carol"..](dictionary encoded) city: ["NYC","LA","NYC",...] (RLE: NYC x3, LA x2, ...) age: [30, 25, 35, ...] (delta encoded) -> sum(age) reads ONLY age column, 1/N the I/O -> 5-10x compression, 10-100x scan speed ``` ### Walkthrough 1. Clients connect to the AG listener (a virtual network name) using T-SQL over TDS (Tabular Data Stream) protocol. The listener routes read-write connections to the primary replica and read-only connections to a synchronous secondary, offloading read load. Authentication can be Windows (Kerberos via Active Directory) or SQL logins; Windows auth is preferred for enterprise SSO. 2. The engine stores data as rowstore B-Trees (OLTP, point lookups) or columnstore (OLAP, scans); In-Memory OLTP tables live in RAM with lock-free MVCC for extreme throughput. The planner chooses between row mode and batch mode (columnstore) based on the query and indexes. 3. The primary streams transaction log (equivalent to WAL/binlog) to secondaries; synchronous secondaries ack before commit (zero data loss), asynchronous secondaries ack later (small DR window). On primary failure, the AG automatically promotes a sync secondary in 5-30 seconds; the listener reroutes traffic transparently.

sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Microsoft SQL Server feature mock using sqlite3 (T-SQL-style).
- T-SQL has DECLARE @x, IF/WHILE, TRY/CATCH. sqlite has none natively, but we can use Python-side logic to mimic the same pattern (the database becomes…
- MERGE: UPSERT in one statement.
- Mock AG: primary + sync secondary + async secondary.
- 1. T-SQL procedural extensions (sqlite UDFs)
- 2. MERGE (UPSERT) + OUTPUT clause
- SQLite uses UPSERT (ON CONFLICT) -- conceptually same as MERGE
- 3. Always On Availability Group simulation

**Defines:** `demo_tsql_procedural()`, `demo_merge_output()`, `Replica`, `AvailabilityGroup`, `demo_columnstore()`

```python
"""
Microsoft SQL Server feature mock using sqlite3 (T-SQL-style).
Demonstrates: T-SQL procedural extensions, MERGE (UPSERT), OUTPUT
clause, Always On AG replica simulation, columnstore vs rowstore
scan comparison, and Windows-auth-style login.

Run:  python3 sqlserver_demo.py
"""

import sqlite3
import time
import random
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Optional

# ---------- 1. T-SQL procedural extensions (sqlite UDFs) ----------
def demo_tsql_procedural():
    """T-SQL has DECLARE @x, IF/WHILE, TRY/CATCH. sqlite has none
    natively, but we can use Python-side logic to mimic the same
    pattern (the database becomes 'programmable' via app code)."""
    print("=== 1. T-SQL procedural extension (mimicked) ===")
    print("  -- T-SQL stored procedure (real SQL Server syntax):")
    print("  CREATE PROCEDURE UpdateBalance")
    print("      @UserId INT, @Amount DECIMAL(10,2)")
    print("  AS")
    print("  BEGIN")
    print("      BEGIN TRY")
    print("          BEGIN TRANSACTION;")
    print("          UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance + @Amount")
    print("              WHERE UserId = @UserId;")
    print("          IF @@ROWCOUNT = 0")
    print("              INSERT INTO Accounts(UserId, Balance)")
    print("              VALUES(@UserId, @Amount);")
    print("          COMMIT;")
    print("      END TRY")
    print("      BEGIN CATCH")
    print("          ROLLBACK;")
    print("          THROW;")
    print("      END CATCH")
    print("  END")
    print("  -> Business logic in DB: zero round-trips")

# ---------- 2. MERGE (UPSERT) + OUTPUT clause ----------
def demo_merge_output():
    """MERGE: UPSERT in one statement. OUTPUT: returns affected rows."""
    print("\n=== 2. MERGE (UPSERT) + OUTPUT clause ===")
    conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    conn.execute("CREATE TABLE accounts(user_id INT PRIMARY KEY, balance REAL)")
    conn.executemany("INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (?,?)", [(1, 100.0), (2, 50.0)])

    # SQLite uses UPSERT (ON CONFLICT) -- conceptually same as MERGE
    print("  MERGE accounts AS t USING (VALUES (1, 25.0), (3, 75.0)) AS s(uid, amt)")
    print("  ON t.user_id = s.uid WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET balance += s.amt")
    print("                       WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT VALUES(s.uid, s.amt)")
    print("  OUTPUT $action, inserted.user_id, inserted.balance;")

    # Mimic in sqlite
    conn.executemany(
        "INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (?,?) ON CONFLICT(user_id) "
        "DO UPDATE SET balance = balance + ?",
        [(1, 25.0, 25.0), (3, 75.0, 75.0)])
    conn.commit()
    rows = conn.execute("SELECT * FROM accounts ORDER BY user_id").fetchall()
    print(f"  Result: {rows}")
    print("  OUTPUT clause returns: [('UPDATE', 1, 125.0), ('INSERT', 3, 75.0)]")

# ---------- 3. Always On Availability Group simulation ----------
@dataclass
class Replica:
    name: str
    role: str           # "primary" or "secondary"
    commit_mode: str    # "sync" or "async"
    data: dict = field(default_factory=dict)
    acked_lsn: int = 0
    applied_lsn: int = 0

class AvailabilityGroup:
    """Mock AG: primary + sync secondary + async secondary."""

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.replicas = []
        self.current_lsn = 0

    def add_replica(self, r):
        self.replicas.append(r)

    def write(self, key, value):
        self.current_lsn += 1
        lsn = self.current_lsn
        # Primary commits locally
        primary = next(r for r in self.replicas if r.role == "primary")
        primary.data[key] = value
        primary.applied_lsn = lsn

        # Replicate to secondaries
        for r in self.replicas:
            if r.role == "secondary":
                if r.commit_mode == "sync":
                    # Sync: wait for ack before returning
                    r.acked_lsn = lsn
                    # Apply (small delay)
                    time.sleep(0.001)
                    r.data[key] = value
                    r.applied_lsn = lsn
                else:
                    # Async: don't wait, catch up later
                    pass
        return lsn

    def failover(self):
        """Promote a sync secondary to primary."""
        old_primary = next(r for r in self.replicas if r.role == "primary")
        # Find a sync secondary
        candidates = [r for r in self.replicas
                      if r.role == "secondary" and r.commit_mode == "sync"]
        if not candidates:
            raise RuntimeError("No sync secondary for failover")
        new_primary = max(candidates, key=lambda r: r.applied_lsn)
        old_primary.role = "secondary"
        old_primary.commit_mode = "sync"
        new_primary.role = "primary"
        return new_primary

# ---------- 4. Columnstore vs rowstore scan ----------
def demo_columnstore():
    """Mock: rowstore reads all columns; columnstore reads only needed."""
    print("\n=== 4. Columnstore vs rowstore scan ===")
    n_rows = 100_000
    # Generate data: 10 columns
    data = [{
        "id": i, "user": f"user_{i}", "city": ["NYC", "LA", "SF", "BOS"][i % 4],
        "age": 20 + (i % 60), "salary": 30_000 + (i % 70_000),
        "dept": i % 20, "title": f"title_{i % 50}", "yoe": i % 30,
        "level": i % 6, "remote": i % 2 == 0,
    } for i in range(n_rows)]

    # Rowstore scan: SELECT SUM(age) FROM employees
    # Reads ALL columns (no column pruning)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    total = 0
    for row in data:
        # Touch all 10 columns to mimic rowstore read pattern
        _ = (row["id"], row["user"], row["city"], row["age"], row["salary"],
             row["dept"], row["title"], row["yoe"], row["level"], row["remote"])
        total += row["age"]
    rowstore_ms = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000

    # Columnstore scan: SELECT SUM(age) FROM employees
    # Reads ONLY age column
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    total2 = sum(row["age"] for row in data)
    columnstore_ms = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000

    print(f"  Table: {n_rows} rows, 10 columns")
    print(f"  Query: SELECT SUM(age) FROM employees")
    print(f"  Rowstore (read all 10 cols):    {rowstore_ms:.2f} ms")
    print(f"  Columnstore (read age col only): {columnstore_ms:.2f} ms")
    print(f"  Speedup: ~{rowstore_ms/max(columnstore_ms,0.001):.1f}x "
          f"(in real SQL Server: 10-100x with batch mode + compression)")

# ---------- Demo ----------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo_tsql_procedural()
    demo_merge_output()

    print("\n=== 3. Always On Availability Group ===")
    ag = AvailabilityGroup("ag-prod")
    primary = Replica("node-1", "primary", "sync")
    sync_sec = Replica("node-2", "secondary", "sync")
    async_sec = Replica("node-3", "secondary", "async")
    ag.add_replica(primary)
    ag.add_replica(sync_sec)
    ag.add_replica(async_sec)

    lsn = ag.write("user:1", {"balance": 1000})
    print(f"  Wrote user:1 -> LSN {lsn}")
    print(f"    Primary (node-1): applied LSN {primary.applied_lsn}")
    print(f"    Sync Sec (node-2): acked={sync_sec.acked_lsn}, "
          f"applied={sync_sec.applied_lsn}")
    print(f"    Async Sec (node-3): acked={async_sec.acked_lsn}, "
          f"applied={async_sec.applied_lsn} (lagging)")

    print("\n  Failover: primary node-1 dies -> promote node-2")
    new_p = ag.failover()
    print(f"    New primary: {new_p.name}")
    print(f"    Zero data loss (node-2 was sync, acked LSN {sync_sec.applied_lsn})")
    print(f"    AG listener reroutes clients transparently in 5-30s")

    demo_columnstore()
```
